title: God is shared in, not sharing
source_text: Πάλιν δὲ αυ ἑαυτῷ συνείρει πλείονα λέγων ὡς ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν διδόμενα, ἅπερ οὐδεὶς τῶν ἐν Χριστιανοῖς νοῦν ἐχόντων δίδωσιν. οὐ γάρ φησι τὶς ἡμῶν ὅτι μετέχει σχήματος ὁ θεὸς ἢ χρώματος, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ κινήσεως μετέχει ὁ διὰ τὸ ἑστηκέναι καὶ βεβαίαν εἶναι τὴν φύσιν αὐτοῦ προκαλούμενος καὶ τὸν δίκαιον ἐπὶ τὰ παραπλήσια καὶ λέγων· „σὺ δὲ αὐτοῦ στῆθι μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ.“ εἰ δέ τινες λέξεις οἱονεὶ κίνησίν τινα παριστᾶσιν αὐτοῦ, ὡς καὶ ἡ λέγουσα· „ἤκουσαν κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ περιπατοῦντος ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τὸ δειλινὸν,“ οὕτως ἀκουστέον τῶν τοιούτων ὡς κινουμένου νοουμένου τοῦ θεοῦ τοῖς ἡμαρτηκόσιν, ἢ οὕτως ἀκουστέον τῶν τοιούτων ὡς καὶ ὕπνου θεοῦ τροπικῶς λεγομένου ἢ ὀργῆς ἤ τινος τῶν παραπλησίων. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ οὐσίας μετέχει ὁ θεός· μετέχεται γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ μετέχει, καὶ μετέχεται ὑπὸ τῶν ἐχόντων „πνεῦμα θεοῦ“. καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν οὐ μετέχει μὲν δικαιοσύνης, „δικαιοσύνη“ δὲ ὢν μετέχεται ὑπὸ τῶν δικαίων. πολὺς δ᾿ ὁ περὶ τῆς οὐσίας λόγος καὶ δυσθεώρητος καὶ μάλιστα, ἐὰν ἡ κυρίως οὐσία ἡ ἑστῶσα καὶ ἀσώματος ᾖ· ἵν᾿ εὑρεθῇ, πότερον ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας ἐστὶ πρεσβείᾳ καὶ δυνάμει ὁ θεὸς μεταδιδοὺς οὐσίας οἷς μεταδίδωσι κατὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ λόγον καὶ αὐτῷ λόγῳ, ἢ καὶ αὐτός ἐστιν οὐσία, πλὴν τῇ φύσει ἀόρατος λέγεται ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος λόγῳ φάσκοντι· „ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου,“ σημαίνεται δὲ ἐκ τῆς „ἀοράτου“ φωνῆς ὁ ἀσώματος. ζητητέον δὲ καὶ, εἰ οὐσίαν μὲν οὐσιῶν λεκτέον καὶ ἰδέαν ἰδεῶν καὶ ἀρχὴν τὸν μονογενῆ καὶ πρωτότοκον „πάσης κτίσεως“ ἐπέκεινα δὲ πάντων τούτων τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ θεόν.
pass_a_gloss: Again he strings together (συνείρω) for himself more things, saying [them] as granted (δίδωμι) by us, which none of those among Christians having sense (νοῦς) grants. For none of us says that God partakes (μετέχω) of shape (σχῆμα) or colour (χρῶμα); but neither does he partake of motion (κίνησις), he who because of standing (ἵστημι, pf.) and his nature (φύσις) being firm (βέβαιος) calls forth (προκαλέομαι) also the righteous one (δίκαιος) to similar things, saying 'But you stand here with me.' If some sayings (λέξις) as it were present some motion of him, as the one saying 'They heard the Lord God walking (περιπατέω) in the paradise in the evening (δειλινόν)', such must be heard as of God being thought to move for those who have sinned (ἁμαρτάνω), or must be heard as also sleep (ὕπνος) of God is said figuratively (τροπικῶς), or anger (ὀργή) or something similar. But neither does God partake of substance (οὐσία); for he is partaken of (μετέχεται, pass.) rather than partakes, and is partaken of by those having Spirit of God. And our Saviour does not partake of righteousness (δικαιοσύνη), but being righteousness is partaken of by the righteous. Much (πολύς) is the discourse about substance and hard to contemplate (δυσθεώρητος), especially if substance properly (κυρίως) is the stable (ἑστῶσα) and incorporeal (ἀσώματος); so that it be found whether God is beyond (ἐπέκεινα) substance in seniority/dignity (πρεσβεία) and power (δύναμις), giving a share (μεταδίδωμι) of substance to those to whom he gives according to his own Word (λόγος) and to the Word himself, or he too is substance, except he is said invisible (ἀόρατος) in nature in the saying about the Saviour: 'who is image of the invisible God'; and from the word 'invisible' the incorporeal is signified. It must be inquired (ζητητέον) also whether one should call the only-begotten (μονογενής) and firstborn of all creation substance of substances and idea of ideas (ἰδέα ἰδεῶν) and principle (ἀρχή), and beyond all these his Father and God.
pass_b_english: Once again he strings together a number of points, stating them as though we granted them, though no Christian of sense grants them. For none of us says that God shares in shape or colour. Nor does he share in motion: it is because he stands firm and his nature is steadfast that he calls the righteous man too to the same, saying, “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). And if some passages seem to describe a kind of motion in him, such as the one that says, “They heard the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening” (Genesis 3:8), we must understand such passages to mean that God is thought of as moving by those who have sinned; or we must understand them in the same way as when sleep, or anger, or anything of the kind is ascribed to God figuratively.

Nor, again, does God share in substance. For he is shared in rather than sharing, and he is shared in by those who have “the Spirit of God” (Romans 8:9). Our Saviour, too, does not share in righteousness; rather, being “righteousness” (1 Corinthians 1:30), he is shared in by the righteous.

The question of substance is a large one and hard to see into, above all if substance in the proper sense is what is stable and incorporeal. We would need to find out whether God is “beyond substance in dignity and power” (Plato, Republic 509b), imparting substance to those to whom he imparts it according to his own Word, and to the Word himself; or whether he too is substance, though he is called invisible in nature in the passage about the Saviour that says, “who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), where the word “invisible” signifies the incorporeal. We must also inquire whether the only-begotten, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), is to be called substance of substances, idea of ideas, and first principle, while his Father and God is beyond all these.

choices.choice: No direct quotation of Celsus is marked in this chapter: Origen restates Celsus’s negations (shape, colour, motion, substance) in his own sentences, so Pass B does not put them in quotation marks. ‘Stating them as though we granted them’ renders λέγων ὡς ὑφ’ ἡμῶν διδόμενα; the sense may be that Celsus presents as Christian concessions points no sensible Christian concedes. μετέχω rendered ‘share in’ throughout to keep Origen’s active/passive play (μετέχει / μετέχεται). Deuteronomy 5:31 LXX σὺ δὲ αὐτοῦ στῆθι μετ’ ἐμοῦ matches. Genesis 3:8 LXX (ἤκουσαν τῆς φωνῆς κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ περιπατοῦντος ...); Origen omits ‘the voice’. ‘Sleep of God’ is an uncited general allusion, possibly Psalm 44:23 (LXX 43:24) or Psalm 78:65 (LXX 77:65); not cited inline as uncertain. ‘Having the Spirit of God’ cited to Romans 8:9 (πνεῦμα θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ... πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ οὐκ ἔχει); 1 Corinthians 7:40 (πνεῦμα θεοῦ ἔχειν) is the closest wording and an equal candidate. 1 Corinthians 1:30: Christ made our righteousness. Plato, Republic 509b: ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας πρεσβείᾳ καὶ δυνάμει ὑπερέχοντος, near-verbatim; Origen’s sentence lacks ὑπερέχοντος, so Pass B quotes only what Origen wrote. ‘According to his own Word, and to the Word himself’ renders κατὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ λόγον καὶ αὐτῷ λόγῳ (dative read as a second recipient of substance). ἀρχή rendered ‘first principle’.

'for he stands firm ... and he even calls the righteous man to be like him' -> 'it is because he stands firm and his nature is steadfast that he calls the righteous man too to the same' (restores διὰ τό causal link; ἐπὶ τὰ παραπλήσια is 'to the like', not 'to be like him')
Plato quotation trimmed to 'beyond substance in dignity and power': 'surpassing it' came from Plato's ὑπερέχοντος, which Origen's Greek does not have
